spoken: Fire tiny particles, one at a time, at a wall with two narrow slits in it.
Each one lands on the screen behind as a single dot.
At first, the dots seem to land almost anywhere.
But keep going, and they sort themselves into stripes.
Stripes like these are what waves make when they overlap.
So what went through the slits? Was it a particle, or a wave?
This is the double-slit experiment.
For centuries, people argued about what light actually is.
In his Treatise on Light, of 1690, Christiaan Huygens described it as a wave.
Isaac Newton's Opticks, published in 1704, leaned toward particles.
In later editions he asked, are not the rays of light very small bodies, emitted from shining substances?
Newton's reputation was so great that, through the eighteenth century, the particle view held a wide lead.
So how could you tell a wave from a stream of particles?
Send particles through two slits, and you'd expect two bright bands, one behind each slit.
But waves can do something particles can't. When they meet, they can add up, or cancel out.
Crest on crest makes a bigger wave; crest on trough makes nothing at all. That's interference.
Thomas Young was a British doctor and polymath, who later helped decipher the Rosetta Stone.
On the 24th of November, 1803, he described an experiment anyone could repeat, whenever the sun shines.
He let sunlight in through a small hole, and held a card a thirtieth of an inch wide in the beam.
In its shadow appeared coloured fringes, which were stripes of light and dark.
When he blocked the light on one side of the card, the fringes vanished.
So the fringes needed light from both sides, meeting and interfering.
His lectures, published in 1807, describe the version we know, with light through two narrow slits.
Whether he ever actually did it with two slits is not clear.
The turn came in 1818, when Augustin Fray-nel entered a French prize contest with a wave theory of light.
One judge, Simeon Pwasson, spotted what looked like an absurd prediction.
In the middle of a small round disc's shadow, it said, there should be a bright spot.
The head of the judges, Fran-swah Arago, tried it, and there was the spot.
After that, most scientists accepted that light is a wave.
In 1865, James Clark Maxwell predicted it is an electromagnetic wave, and the particle idea seemed finished.
So how do two slits make so many stripes?
Each slit acts as a new source, sending out waves that spread in circles.
To reach a point on the screen, one wave usually travels a little farther than the other.
If the extra distance is a whole number of wavelengths, crests arrive together, and that spot is bright.
If it's half a wavelength, crest meets trough, and the spot is dark.
Move along the screen and the extra distance grows steadily, so the stripes go bright, dark, bright, dark.
The spacing of the stripes is the wavelength, times the distance to the screen, divided by the gap between the slits.
Take slits half a millimetre apart, light with a wavelength of zero point six micrometres, and a screen one metre away.
The stripes come out one point two millimetres apart.
Move the screen twice as far away, and they spread twice as wide.
Young had described this too, with stripes wider also in the same proportion as the apertures are closer to each other.
He used fringes like these to estimate the wavelengths of different colours, close to modern values.
But the wave picture had a crack in it.
In 1905, Albert Einstein proposed that light's energy comes in separate lumps, now called photons.
So what happens to the stripes when light is so dim that it arrives a little at a time?
In 1909, a young Cambridge physicist, Geoffrey Ingram Taylor, tried it.
He dimmed a gas light with dark glass, until it was like a candle more than a mile away.
The light passed a sewing needle onto a photographic plate, which took three months to expose.
The fringes were still there.
As Paul Dirac later put it, each photon then interferes only with itself.
One caution is that Taylor's paper never mentions photons, and his dim lamp wasn't a true single-photon source.
That test came in 1986, when a French team including Alain Aspect used a genuine single-photon source and an interferometer.
The interference was still there, one photon at a time.
Each photon is detected at one single point.
A few hundred look like noise.
By ten thousand, the stripes are unmistakable.
Brighter light just makes the dots pile up faster, giving the same pattern, sooner.
Electrons came the other way round. From 1897, experiments showed them behaving as particles.
Then, in 1924, Louis de Broy proposed that all matter has a wave side too.
Experiments in 1927 confirmed it, bouncing electrons off crystals and through thin films.
But for decades, the two-slit version with electrons was taught only as a thought experiment.
This experiment, Richard Feynman wrote in his famous lectures, has never been done in just this way.
In fact it had, in 1961, the year those lectures began.
Klaus Yernsson, in Tubingen, made slits for electrons and saw the fringes, with up to five slits.
In 1974, in Bologna, Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi sent electrons through one at a time.
Instead of slits they used an electron biprism, which is a fine wire that splits the beam in two.
In 1989, Akira Tonomura and colleagues at Hitachi made it cleaner still.
Fewer than 1,000 electrons arrived each second, so two were never in the apparatus at once.
Each one arrived as a single flash. Here are 8 electrons, then 270, then 2,000.
Over a twenty-minute exposure, 60,000 electrons drew the stripes.
In 2002, Physics World readers voted the single-electron version the most beautiful experiment in physics.
How big can a thing be and still do this?
In 1991, helium atoms interfered after passing through slits in gold foil.
In 1999, a team in Vienna sent buckyballs, molecules of 60 carbon atoms, through a grating of many slits.
A buckyball is zero point seven nanometres across; its wave was some 280 times smaller, and still it interfered.
The record grew to molecules of 810 atoms in 2013, and about 2,000 atoms in 2019.
In 2026, a team in Vienna showed interference with sodium clusters, some of more than 7,000 atoms.
The heavier the object, the shorter its wave, and the harder its stripes are to see.
So far, quantum theory has passed every one of these tests.
Now comes the most famous twist.
Put a detector at each slit, to find out which one each particle goes through.
Every particle is found at one slit or the other, never split between them.
And the stripes vanish.
The screen shows two single-slit patterns, simply added together, with no interference.
Why? To learn the path, the detector has to interact with the particle.
That leaves a record of which way it went, and the two paths can no longer interfere.
It's often told as if a conscious observer changes the outcome, but the standard account needs no mind at all.
What matters is whether the path could be known, in principle, from anything left behind.
In 2004, a Vienna team laser-heated carbon-70 molecules, so they gave off heat radiation in flight.
That radiation carried traces of each molecule's path, and the hotter the molecules, the fainter the stripes.
Nobody looked at that light; it only had to exist.
And it isn't all or nothing. A 1987 experiment gathered some path information and kept fainter stripes.
The better the two paths can be told apart, the fainter the stripes have to be.
Richard Feynman put this experiment at the centre of quantum physics.
He called it impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way.
It has in it the heart of quantum mechanics, he said. In reality, it contains the only mystery.
Quantum mechanics describes each particle with a wave that passes through both slits.
The wave only sets the odds of where each particle lands, and those odds are the square of the wave at each spot.
Each detection is still a single dot, and only the pile of dots reveals the wave.
What happens in between is where interpretations of quantum mechanics part ways.
Some say the question of which slit means nothing without a detector; others picture many worlds, or a guiding wave.
But they all predict the same stripes, dot for dot.
Young's stripes showed light is a wave; single dots showed it arrives in lumps.
And a record of the path, of any kind, wipes the stripes away.
With two slits, a screen, and one dot at a time, it's still the clearest view we have of the quantum world.
